meta.titre: Conservation of energy: tracing energy changes step by step
meta.sous_theme: Energy transformations, kinetic and potential energy, efficiency

sections.contenu_markdown: When a mango falls from a tree in a Douala compound, it speeds up as it drops and hits the ground with a thud, a bit of sound and a tiny rise in temperature. Where did its energy go? In a solar lamp sold at the market, sunlight ends up as light at night. Every device you meet is a way of changing energy from one form to another. The GCE examiners ask you to state the law of conservation of energy, name the energy changes in a device, and calculate kinetic energy, potential energy and efficiency.

items: Energy is measured in joules (J) and power is the rate of transferring energy, measured in watts (W).
Work done by a force is the force multiplied by the distance moved in the direction of the force.
The acceleration of free fall is taken as $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ near the Earth's surface.

sections.titre: The law of conservation of energy and its calculations
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Law of conservation of energy.** Energy can neither be created nor destroyed. It can only be changed from one form to another, so the total energy of an isolated system stays constant.

**Forms of energy:** kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, chemical, electrical, thermal (heat), light, sound and nuclear.

**Work and energy.** Work done $W = Fd$ is the energy transferred by a force. Lifting a load or stretching a spring stores energy; friction turns it into heat.

| Energy | Formula | Variables |
|---|---|---|
| Kinetic energy | $E_k = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ | $m$ in kg, $v$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ |
| Gravitational potential energy | $E_p = mgh$ | $h$ is the height above the chosen level |
| Work done | $W = Fd$ | $F$ in newtons, $d$ in metres |
| Efficiency | $\dfrac{\text{useful energy output}}{\text{total energy input}} \times 100\%$ | never more than 100% |
| Power | $P = \dfrac{E}{t}$ | $E$ in joules, $t$ in seconds |

**Wasted energy** is not lost from the universe. It spreads out as heat, and sound, in the surroundings and cannot easily be reused. That is why efficiency is always less than 100%.

variantes.quand_utiliser: when you must name the energy conversion of a device or process
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Name the input form, then the useful output form, then the wasted form.

| Device | Input energy | Useful output | Wasted energy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Solar cell | light | electrical | heat |
| Loudspeaker | electrical | sound | heat |
| Charcoal stove | chemical | heat and light | heat to the air |
| Dynamo | kinetic | electrical | heat, sound |
| Torch with batteries | chemical | light | heat |

variantes.quand_utiliser: when a body moves up or down and air resistance is ignored or small
variantes.contenu_markdown:
If friction and air resistance are negligible, the loss in potential energy equals the gain in kinetic energy:

$$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad v = \sqrt{2gh}$$

The mass cancels, so the speed does not depend on the mass. At the top of the path the object has maximum potential energy and minimum kinetic energy; at the lowest point it is the other way round. If some energy is changed to heat by resistance, then $E_p$ lost $= E_k$ gained $+$ heat produced, and heat produced $= $ resistive force $\times$ distance.

variantes.quand_utiliser: when a motor, engine or crane is described
variantes.contenu_markdown: Efficiency $= \dfrac{\text{useful output}}{\text{input}} \times 100\%$, where the output and the input can both be given as energy or both as power. The useful output of a lifting machine is the gain in potential energy $mgh$. The difference between input and useful output is the wasted energy.

sections.enonce_markdown: A mango of mass $0.40\,\mathrm{kg}$ falls from a branch $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$ above the ground. (a) Calculate its speed just before it hits the ground, ignoring air resistance. (b) In practice its kinetic energy just before impact is only $14\,\mathrm{J}$. Find the energy transferred to the surroundings and the average resistive force of the air.

etapes.action: Calculate the potential energy lost in the fall.
etapes.justification: The mango loses gravitational potential energy $mgh$ as it falls.

etapes.action: Apply conservation of energy for the ideal case.
etapes.justification: With no air resistance, all the lost potential energy becomes kinetic energy: $\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = 20$.

etapes.action: Find the energy that went into the surroundings.
etapes.justification: Total energy is conserved: $E_p$ lost $= E_k$ gained $+$ energy transferred to heat and sound.
The energy lost to the surroundings equals the work done against air resistance, $W = Fd$.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Without air resistance the mango would land at $10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. In reality $6\,\mathrm{J}$ is shared among the mango and the air as heat, which corresponds to an average air resistance of $1.2\,\mathrm{N}$.

items.erreur_markdown: When a ball stops rolling, its energy has been used up.
items.pourquoi_faux: Energy cannot be destroyed. The kinetic energy of the ball has been changed into heat (and a little sound) by friction. The energy is still there but spread in the surroundings.
items.correction_markdown: Say that the kinetic energy was converted to thermal energy by friction, and the total energy is unchanged.

items.erreur_markdown: A heavier stone falls faster because it has more potential energy.
items.pourquoi_faux: In $mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ the mass cancels, so $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ is the same for all masses (when air resistance is negligible). The heavier stone has more energy to convert but also more mass to accelerate.
items.correction_markdown: The speed depends on the height fallen, not on the mass.

items.erreur_markdown: A machine with an input of $400\,\mathrm{J}$ and a useful output of $500\,\mathrm{J}$ has an efficiency of $125\%$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The useful output can never be larger than the input, otherwise energy would be created. The values were exchanged.
items.correction_markdown: Efficiency $= \dfrac{\text{output}}{\text{input}} \times 100\% = \dfrac{400}{500} \times 100\% = 80\%$ if the input is the larger value.

items.erreur_markdown: Calculating kinetic energy with $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv$ or forgetting to square the speed.
items.pourquoi_faux: Kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed. Doubling the speed multiplies the kinetic energy by 4.
items.correction_markdown: Always use $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ and square $v$ before multiplying.

items.erreur_markdown: Using the mass in grams in $mgh$ or $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The joule is defined with the mass in kilograms. A mass of $400\,\mathrm{g}$ used as $400$ makes the answer 1000 times too large.

items.enonce_markdown: Calculate the kinetic energy of a car of mass $1200\,\mathrm{kg}$ moving at $15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

A crane motor takes $2500\,\mathrm{W}$ from the supply and lifts a load of mass $250\,\mathrm{kg}$ through a height of $12\,\mathrm{m}$ in $20\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate (a) the useful work done on the load, (b) the useful power output, (c) the efficiency of the crane, and (d) the energy wasted in the $20\,\mathrm{s}$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $W = mgh = 250 \times 10 \times 12$, so **$W = 30\,000\,\mathrm{J}$**.

(b) $P = \dfrac{W}{t} = \dfrac{30\,000}{20}$, so **$P = 1500\,\mathrm{W}$**.

(c) Efficiency $= \dfrac{1500}{2500} \times 100\%$, so **efficiency $= 60\%$**.

(d) Energy input $= 2500 \times 20 = 50\,000\,\mathrm{J}$, so wasted energy $= 50\,000 - 30\,000$, which is **$20\,000\,\mathrm{J}$** (changed to heat and sound).

items.enonce_markdown: A pendulum bob of mass $0.20\,\mathrm{kg}$ is pulled aside so that it is $0.45\,\mathrm{m}$ above its lowest position, then released. Ignore air resistance. (a) Calculate its maximum kinetic energy and maximum speed. (b) Find its speed when it is $0.25\,\mathrm{m}$ above the lowest position. (c) Describe what happens to the energy of the bob after it has swung for a long time and has come to rest.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) At the lowest point all the potential energy is kinetic: $E_k = mgh = 0.20 \times 10 \times 0.45$, so **$E_k = 0.90\,\mathrm{J}$**. Then $\tfrac{1}{2}(0.20)v^2 = 0.90$, so $v^2 = 9.0$ and **$v = 3.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$**.

(b) At $0.25\,\mathrm{m}$ the potential energy lost from the start corresponds to a drop of $0.45 - 0.25 = 0.20\,\mathrm{m}$. Kinetic energy $= 0.20 \times 10 \times 0.20 = 0.40\,\mathrm{J}$. Then $\tfrac{1}{2}(0.20)v^2 = 0.40$, so $v^2 = 4.0$ and **$v = 2.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$**.

(c) The total of $0.90\,\mathrm{J}$ is gradually changed into heat (in the air and at the support) and a little sound by friction and air resistance. **The energy is conserved, but it is no longer useful.**

items_markdown: **Law of conservation of energy:** energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another.
$E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, $E_p = mgh$ (with $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$), $W = Fd$, $P = E/t$; mass in kg.
For a falling object with negligible resistance, $E_p$ lost $= E_k$ gained, so $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ independent of mass.
Efficiency $= \dfrac{\text{useful output}}{\text{input}} \times 100\%$ and is always less than 100%; wasted energy ends up as heat.
To answer a device question, give input energy, useful output energy and wasted energy.
